heroHeadline: Xiaomi Unveils 3nm Smart-Driving Chip as Domestic AI Chipmakers Post Blowout Growth; Nvidia Denies China-Specific LPU Plan
heroSubtitle: August 24, 2026 — China's domestic silicon buildout kept advancing through the back half of August even as no single event rose to crisis level. On August 17, Shanghai Biren Technology told the Hong Kong Stock Exchange it expects first-half 2026 revenue up as much as 22-fold year-on-year (to $170.8M–$193.1M) with losses narrowing 75-80%, joining a wave of similar guidance from Cambricon and Hygon as US export restrictions continue funneling domestic AI compute demand toward homegrown GPU designers. On August 19, Unitree Robotics surged 460% on its Shanghai STAR Market debut — becoming the first listed humanoid-robot maker in mainland China at a roughly $50B valuation — the same day CNBC and Quartz reported Chinese AI firms including ByteDance, Moonshot AI, Tencent, and Alibaba have been accessing restricted Nvidia chip capacity by renting compute from Southeast Asian data centers, a loophole Congress's stalled Remote Access Security Act aims to close. Alibaba's August 20 earnings showed the tension in that build-out: net income fell 75% year-on-year even as AI capex jumped 75% to nearly $10B and Alibaba Cloud's AI revenue grew 45%. On August 21, Nvidia flatly denied a report by The Information that it planned to ship a China-specific LPU chip — built on technology licensed from Groq — by year-end, stating it has 'no China-specific LPU product in our road map.' Most recently, on August 24, Xiaomi unveiled the Xring D100, which it says is China's first high-computing-power smart-driving chip built on a 3nm process, manufactured by TSMC and capable of running 200-billion-parameter models locally; the chip has completed validation and targets 2027 commercial deployment, backed by more than 21 billion yuan ($3.1B) in Xiaomi chip R&D since the program restarted. Taken together, the past week underscores a steady rather than acute pattern: domestic AI chip designers turning the corner toward profitability, humanoid robotics and EV-adjacent silicon reaching public markets, and the offshore-compute and China-specific-hardware disputes with the US continuing to simmer without a new flashpoint.
